## Paper

## Abstract

Ischemic stroke presents a dual therapeutic challenge, involving dynamic and compartmentalized pathology in both the peripheral immune system and the central nervous system. Departing from conventional holistic treatment strategies, we developed a spatially tiered drug delivery approach using a combination of dual-stiffness nanoparticles (NPs) for compartment-specific therapy. Exploiting stiffness-dependent biodistribution, stiff NPs preferentially targeted peripheral immune cells, delivering anti-inflammatory agents to attenuate systemic inflammation and prevent immune cell infiltration into the brain. In parallel, soft NPs, shielded from immune uptake, efficiently penetrated the brain to deliver neuroprotectants and restore the damaged neural microenvironment. Mechanistic studies indicate that this selective distribution arises from the interplay between NP stiffness-dependent membrane energetics and competitive serum protein adsorption. This mechano-guided delivery strategy achieves synergistic “peripheral-central” intervention via a single administration, establishing a paradigm for precision nanomedicine, with broad potential in treating multi-compartment pathologies.

---

## Introduction

Stroke remains a major global health challenge, with its burden steadily increasing. As of 2021, stroke ranked as the third leading cause of death, following ischemic heart disease and COVID-19, and the fourth leading cause of disability worldwide1. Among all stroke subtypes, ischemic stroke accounts for approximately 87% of cases2, imposing significant medical and economic burdens on both patients and society3.

Crucially, ischemic stroke is not a static or isolated injury but a complex spatially evolving disease, involving both the central nervous system and the peripheral immune compartment3,4. Acute ischemia induces neuronal necrosis, oxidative stress, and blood–brain barrier (BBB) disruption, leading to the leakage of damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) into systemic circulation5–7. These signals activate the peripheral immunity, triggering rapid recruitment of neutrophils and monocytes to the injured brain8,9. The resulting central-peripheral crosstalk forms a self-amplifying inflammatory loop that exacerbates tissue damage and hinders endogenous repair mechanisms.

Despite growing recognition of the spatially compartmentalized pathology of ischemic stroke, most therapeutic strategies have continued to treat the brain and peripheral immune system as a unified target, aiming primarily for systemic immunomodulation or brain-wide neuroprotection10–13. For instance, one approach utilized PEGylated liposomes loaded with atorvastatin to enhance targeted drug delivery to ischemic brain tissue, resulting in improved neuroprotective outcomes10. Another strategy employed macrophage membrane-coated manganese dioxide (MnO₂) nanoparticles (NPs) loaded with fingolimod (FTY), which not only reduced oxidative stress but also promoted the phenotypic transition of microglia to the anti-inflammatory M2 type, thereby modulating the inflammatory microenvironment in ischemic stroke13. While these interventions offer partial benefits, their single-modality nature limits the ability to simultaneously suppress peripheral immune infiltration and facilitate neuronal repair. Moreover, the highly activated peripheral immune response during ischemic stroke accelerates the clearance of exogenous NPs, significantly compromising their targeting efficiency. These limitations may explain the modest clinical success of prior nanotherapeutic efforts to date.

To address these limitations, we developed dual-stiffness NP combination strategy, a spatially resolved therapeutic approach that independently targets i) the periphery and ii) the brain as distinct yet interacting compartments, each requiring tailored intervention (Fig. 1, 2a). NPs have transformed drug delivery by enabling programmable control over physicochemical properties such as size, charge, and surface ligands14–17. Our recent studies have identified NP stiffness, defined as the mechanical resistance to deformation under stress18, as a critical parameter influencing NP-cell interactions and cellular internalization19–21. Indeed, stiffness modulation has also been explored in cancer nanotherapy to improve treatment specificity and efficacy 22–24. Building on these insights, we engineered a mechano-guided NP system combining two types of NPs with distinct stiffness profiles. Rather than employing a uniform NP design, this dual-stiffness approach exploits differential uptake behavior to achieve compartment-specific delivery. When tested in a multilayer barrier model, stiff NPs were preferentially taken up by immune cells, while simultaneously shielding soft NPs from immune clearance and enhancing their uptake by neuronal cells. Leveraging this behavior, we loaded stiff NPs with the anti-inflammatory agent piceatannol (Pic) to suppress systemic immune overactivation and reduce the infiltration of neutrophils and monocytes into the brain. In parallel, the soft NPs carried the neuroprotective compound DL-3-n-butylphthalide (NBP), enabling efficient transport across the BBB and promoting neural repair and local microenvironmental restoration.

In a murine middle cerebral artery occlusion/reperfusion (MCAO/R) model, the drug-loaded dual-stiffness NPs strategy led to a substantial therapeutic benefit, increasing 28-day survival rates from 11.1% to 77.8%, while significantly improving neurological function. This approach not only addresses the spatially divergent pathophysiology of ischemic stroke but also presents a broadly applicable stiffness-graded delivery platform for treating other complex diseases, spatially partitioned diseases, such as Alzheimer’s disease or cerebral gliomas 25.

---

## Results

Preparation and characterization of the dual-stiffness NPs
To construct the dual-stiffness NPs system, we selected two FDA-approved materials, liposomes and poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA). To ensure identical surface properties while achieving distinct mechanical stiffness, Liposomes were prepared as the soft NPs, while PLGA NPs coated with the same lipids (Lipo-PLGA) serve as the stiff counterpart (Fig. 2b). Liposomes were synthesized using a thin-film dispersion and ultrasonic hydration method. Lipo-PLGA NPs were prepared by microfluidics. By optimizing the synthesis parameters, we successfully integrated PLGA cores into liposomes without significantly altering particle size or zeta potential. The resulting Lipo-PLGA NPs exhibited an average size of 123.67 ± 2.52 nm, compared to 130.83 ± 1.01 nm for Liposome (Fig. 2c), both with a polydispersity index (PDI) of below 0.2, indicating uniform size distribution. The zeta potential of Lipo-PLGA is -30 ± 2.91 mV, comparable to that of Liposome (-34.5 ± 4.26 mV) (Fig. 2d). Transmission electron microscope (TEM) revealed the morphology of Lipo-PLGA (Fig. 2e) and Liposome (Fig. 2f), with the confocal imaging showing colocalization of both PLGA cores (DiI-labeled) and lipid shells (DiD-labeled, Pearson’s coefficient: 0.89 ± 0.05; yellow overlay in Supplementary Fig. 1). Atomic force microscopy (AFM) further demonstrated minimal deformation of Lipo-PLGA (Young's modulus of 14.08 ± 3.23 GPa) under mechanical probing, in contrast to significant deformation of Liposome (439.19 ± 82.06 kPa), confirming the enhanced stiffness in Lipo-PLGA (Fig. 2g). Endocytosis pathway assays demonstrated that incorporating a PLGA core preserves the internalization mechanism of both Liposome and Lipo-PLGA, confirming clathrin-mediated endocytosis as their main cellular entry route (Fig. 2h). This indicated that stiff Lipo-PLGA and soft Liposome share identical cellular entry mechanisms, given their similar size, surface charge, and composition. Subsequently, Lipo-PLGA and Liposome were designed as models of stiff and soft NPs, respectively, to systematically investigate the influence of NP stiffness on their in vitro and in vivo fate.

Cellular uptake efficiency of dual-stiffness NPs combination and cell selective preference
We next investigated the differences in the uptake efficiency of NPs with varying stiffness across different cell lines. Upon co-incubation with the immune cell line Raw264.7 cells, stiff NPs consistently exhibited significantly higher cellular uptake than the soft NPs (Supplementary Fig. 2, Fig. 3a). Notably, the intracellular accumulation of stiff NPs after 1 h incubation was equivalent to that of the soft NPs after 4 h, demonstrating faster and more efficient internalization of stiff NPs by Raw264.7 cells. Similarly, another immune cell line BV2 showed comparable stiffness-dependent uptake disparity (Fig. 3b), with significantly elevated uptake of stiff NPs over the soft ones. In contrast, the neuronal cell line PC12 displayed the opposite preference under identical conditions, revealed 1.5-fold higher endocytosis of the soft NPs compared to their stiff counterparts (Fig. 3c).

We then examined whether co-incubating cells with NPs of both stiffness would lead to differential cellular uptake efficiency. Notably, under co-administration conditions, stiff NPs exhibited 1.2-fold increase in accumulation within immune cells compared to single-NP administration (Fig. 3d), whereas soft NPs achieved ~50% evasion from immune clearance (Fig. 3e).

The distinct uptake behavior induced by differences in NP stiffness offer a strategy for spatially stratified drug delivery using a dual-stiffness NP combination. To test this hypothesis, we established an in vitro dual-compartment model with spatially separated neutrophils and PC12 cells (Fig. 3f). The dual-stiffness NP combination significantly enhanced the uptake of stiff NPs by the upper-layer neutrophils, resulting in fewer stiff NPs reaching the lower compartment for uptake by PC12 cells (Fig. 3g). Meanwhile, the shielding effect on soft NPs markedly reduced their uptake by neutrophils, thereby facilitating their penetration into the lower compartment and enhancing uptake by PC12 cells (Fig. 3h). These results indicated that the dual-stiffness NPs exploit the differential cellular uptake behaviors of stiff and soft NPs, achieving passive targeting to different cell types in separate compartments through a single administration. Specifically, immune cells preferentially engulf stiff NPs, while neural cells predominantly uptake soft NPs.

To explore the underlying mechanism, we performed coarse-grained molecular dynamics (CGMD) simulations of NP-membrane interactions (Fig. 3i-k, Supplementary Movie 1). The free energy landscape obtained from steered molecular dynamics (SMD) revealed that soft NPs benefit from stronger adhesion but require deeper penetration (43.6 nm) and nearly twice the total energy cost (538.8 𝑘 𝑇) compared to stiff NPs (274.6 𝑘 𝑇). Soft NPs benefit from enhanced adhesion due to deformability, yet their compliance ultimately imposes higher energy penalties during internalization. In contrast, stiff NPs exhibit pronounced thermodynamic advantages after membrane contact, consuming less energy for full engulfment.

We further investigated how intrinsic cell mechanics influence this stiffness-dependent behavior. Neuronal cells such as PC12 are softer26 and possess a more diffuse actin network, reflecting their need for dynamic material exchange27,28, whereas immune cells are stiffer29 and exhibit actin–myosin enrichment at the membrane to support rapid phagocytosis30,31. Consistent with this, actin staining showed strong cortical enrichment in Raw264.7 cells but loose distribution in PC12 cells (Fig. 3l,m, Supplementary Fig. 3). Because actin polymerization mainly drives the internalization step of endocytosis rather than the initial adhesion, we next used cytochalasin D (CytD) to inhibit actin dynamics and assess its effect on NP uptake. CytD reduced stiff NP uptake in Raw264.7 cells, but had smaller effect on soft NPs or on PC12 uptake overall (Supplementary Fig. 4). This result suggests that stiff NP uptake in Raw264.7 cells is largely dependent on internalization. In contrast, PC12 cells showed negligible changes in NP uptake upon actin inhibition, consistent with their sparse actin networks and limited involvement of internalization.

Taken together, these results establish a mechanistic framework in which NP stiffness dictates membrane deformation energetics, while cellular cytoskeletal organization determines which uptake stage dominates. Their interplay drives cell-type-selective behavior—immune cells favor stiff NPs through efficient internalization, whereas neuronal cells prefer soft NPs due to binding advantages.

To verify this, we decoupled binding and internalization in a two-stage experiment, allowing sufficient binding before internalization to assess which step more critically influences cellular uptake efficiency (Fig. 3n). In Raw264.7 cells (Fig. 3o), stiff NPs maintained their uptake advantages after decoupling two stages, confirming that internalization efficiency governs their uptake preference. In contrast, in PC12 cells (Fig. 3p), uptake of stiff and soft NPs became comparable once binding and internalization were separated, abolishing the original soft NPs preference (Fig. 3c). This demonstrates that PC12 uptake is primarily governed by binding affinity, while immune-cell uptake depends on internalization kinetics. Collectively, these results are consistent with our initial hypothesis and align well with the simulated energetic profiles of NPs with different stiffness.

The fate of NPs with different stiffness in vivo and shielding effect mechanism
We further sought to validate this distinct spatial distribution in vivo. We established an MCAO/R model to simulate ischemic stroke, which causes cerebral hypoxia and metabolic failure, triggering massive neuronal apoptosis and releasing DAMPs into the periphery. Activation of circulating immune cells subsequently triggers rapid internalization of NPs. We then investigated whether combining NPs of different stiffness affects their uptake efficiency by peripheral immune cells. Due to the low abundance of leukocytes in the peripheral blood (0.1–0.2% of total blood cells), we used an integrated in vivo-in vitro approach (Fig. 4a) to avoid the difficulty of detecting sufficient positive immune cells by flow cytometry (Supplementary Fig. 5). This approach obtained disease-state leukocytes ex vivo while amplifying the visibility of stiffness-dependent phagocytic disparities. The results demonstrated that the dual-stiffness NPs enhanced the peripheral leukocytes uptake of the stiff NPs while markedly decreasing that of the soft NPs (Fig. 4b,c). We next traced the biodistribution of the soft NPs under the dual-stiffness regimen. The results showed that the “shielding” soft NPs evaded immune clearance under the protection of stiff NPs, thus significantly enhancing their accumulation in brain tissue (Fig. 4d) and significantly reducing hepatic retention (Fig. 4e). These results indicated that the dual-stiffness NP combination enabled delivery of stiff NPs to the periphery and soft NPs to the brain, creating a spatially tiered drug delivery system.

To understand this phenomenon, we analyzed the protein corona composition of NPs after serum incubation. Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment revealed that stiff NPs were more enriched with complement-related proteins, particularly those involved in the classical pathway (C1 complex, C6), compared with soft NPs (Supplementary Fig. 6, Fig. 4f~g). This indicates that NP stiffness is a key determinant of complement adsorption and immune recognition potential. We further examined the influence of serum complement on NP uptake by immune cells using three serum conditions: serum, heat-inactivated serum (56 °C, 1 h, to inactivate complement), and untreated buffer. Stiff NPs preincubated with serum exhibited significantly higher immune cellular uptake, whereas heat-inactivation largely abolished this enhancement (Fig. 4h). Soft NPs showed a similar trend (Fig. 4i), but the magnitude of serum-induced enhancement was much smaller than that observed for stiff NPs. This suggests that, compared with stiff NPs, soft NPs adsorb fewer complement-related components from serum and therefore experience a weaker complement-mediated increase in immune cell uptake. This trend was further supported by the quantification of C3b in NP protein coronas using ELISA, which revealed higher C3b levels on stiff NPs than on soft NPs (Supplementary Fig. 7).

We then compared the corona composition of each NP type when incubated alone or in dual stiffness NP combination. For stiff NPs (Supplementary Fig. 8, Fig. 4j), co-administration with soft NPs led to an increased enrichment of C1 complex components (C1qa, C1qb, C1s1, C1rb) and decreased levels of complement inhibitory factors (Cfh, Cfhr1, Cfhr2), indicating enhanced complement activation potential. In contrast, soft NPs in the dual-stiffness formulation exhibited substantially reduced adsorption of complement and immunoglobulin proteins (Supplementary Fig. 9, Fig. 4k). These results suggest a competitive adsorption process, where stiff NPs preferentially bind complement proteins, thereby reducing complement deposition on soft NPs. To further confirm this complement-mediated protection, we pre-treated stiff NPs under three serum conditions and combined pre-treated stiff NPs with dye-labeled soft NPs as dual-stiffness NP system. We evaluated immune cell uptake of soft NPs in this system (Fig. 4l). The lowest uptake of soft NPs was observed in serum pre-incubation stiff NPs group, whereas heat-inactivation or untreated stiff NPs groups diminished this effect. This supports the notion that complement activation contributes critically to the shielding behavior.

Beyond the biochemical contribution of complement competition, the shielding effect can also be interpreted from a biophysical perspective. Stiff NPs, which possess lower membrane-wrapping energy barriers and faster engulfment kinetics, are more likely to occupy membrane binding sites and locally deplete curvature resources on immune cells (Fig. 3i-k, Supplementary Movie 1). In addition, as NP internalization by immune cells involves actin cytoskeleton remodeling, we performed CLSM to observe actin organization during NP-cell interaction (Supplementary Fig. 10). After co-incubation with stiff NPs, immune cells exhibited noticeable actin redistribution accompanied by progressive stiff NP internalization, whereas soft NPs induced minimal changes in actin organization. These observations suggest that stiff NPs not only benefit from energetic advantages in membrane wrapping but are also associated with increased engagement of the actin cytoskeleton during uptake. Such enhanced cytoskeletal involvement may reduce the availability of actin polymerization capacity, potentially limiting the phagocytic uptake of subsequently encountered NPs and thereby further reinforcing the complement-mediated shielding effect observed in the dual-stiffness NP system.

We further evaluated the immune cell uptake of NPs under different administration sequences and time intervals, we fluorescently labeled and combined stiff and soft NPs (Supplementary Fig. 11). Specifically, when stiff NPs were added first, immune cells preferentially internalized them due to lower energetic barriers. As a result, subsequently added soft NPs exhibited reduced uptake, with the inhibitory effect becoming more pronounced at shorter dosing intervals (Supplementary Fig. 11 a,b). In contrast, pre-incubation with soft NPs did not significantly affect the uptake of subsequently added stiff NPs, consistent with the lack of a mechanical advantage for soft NPs (Supplementary Fig. 11 c,d). Regarding sequential dosing of the same stiffness NPs, we found that the addition of stiff NPs showed reduced uptake of the second batch, likely due to partial energy depletion from the first phagocytosis. However, shorter intervals increased complement activation, which enhanced the second-batch uptake (Supplementary Fig. 11 e,f). Lastely, sequential soft NP dosing led to reduced uptake of the second batch at shorter intervals, reflecting an “energetic occupation effect” rather than complement-mediated stimulation (Supplementary Fig. 11 g,h).

Collectively, these results suggest that NP stiffness dictates not only individual uptake efficiency but also interparticle competition and sequence-dependent shielding behavior, mediated by both energetic and complement-related mechanisms.

Biofunction of drug-loaded dual-stiffness NPs
After confirming that the dual-stiffness NP combination achieved dual-compartment distribution, we proceeded to load stiff and soft NPs with different agents, targeting the peripheral and central compartments, respectively, to mediate spatially segregated anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective effects.

CD18 (integrin β2), a critical subunit of functional integrins LFA-1 and Mac-132, mediates the binding of peripheral immune cells to vascular endothelial adhesion molecules (e.g., ICAM-1) under ischemic stroke conditions33, promoting massive infiltration of neutrophils, monocytes, and other leukocytes into the brain. The stiff NPs were designed to carry Pic34, a Syk kinase inhibitor (a key regulator of integrin signaling) to downregulate CD18 expression35, thereby suppressing leukocyte adhesion, migration, and peripheral inflammation in ischemic stroke model mice. The encapsulation efficiency of Pic@stiff reached at 68.52 ± 2.32 % (Supplementary Fig. 12a). In vitro release experiment showed that Pic@stiff exhibited an early rapid burst, releasing around 70% of Pic in the first 2 h followed by a slower sustained phase (Supplementary Fig. 13a). Such an early fast-release window aligns well with the acute inflammatory surge and the rapid neutrophil infiltration that occur within hours after ischemic stroke. We employed Pic@stiff to suppress immune cell migration, like neutrophils, into the brain. As outlined in Fig. 5a, the primary neutrophils isolated from mice could penetrate the in vitro BBB model, followed by N-Formyl-Met-Leu-Phe (fMLP) stimulation to induce inflammation. The Pic@stiff treatment significantly reduced CD18 expression on neutrophils, thereby markedly decreasing their transmigration into the lower chamber under inflammatory conditions (Fig. 5b, c). Meanwhile, NBP36,37, a neuroprotectant targeting oxidative stress and apoptosis, was encapsulated in the soft NPs (NBP@soft), achieving an encapsulation efficiency of 77.42 ± 4.89% (Supplementary Fig. 12b). NBP@soft demonstrated a gradual release pattern, with an initial release of 35% within the first 2 h and a continuous diffusion-dominated release that reached around 100% at 24 h (Supplementary Fig. 13b). This sustained release pattern matches the prolonged oxidative stress and delayed neuronal injury that persists during the ischemic stroke, thereby supporting the need for continuous neuroprotection. We further investigated whether NBP@soft could enhance the therapeutic effects of NBP on damaged neuronal cells. The results showed that NBP@soft significantly increased the viability of damaged PC12 cells in vitro compared to free NBP, confirming its enhanced neuroprotective role (Fig. 5d).

Therapeutic effects of drug-loaded dual-stiffness NPs altering their biodistribution
After validating the inhibitory effects of Pic@stiff on immune cell migration and the neuroprotective effects of NBP@soft, we further investigated whether their combination in the final formulation could provide both peripheral anti-inflammatory and central neuroprotective effects in vitro. During the acute phase of ischemic stroke, DAMPs released into the periphery activate immune cells that adhere to cerebral endothelial and infiltrate brain parenchyma—neutrophils infiltration peaks at 2-6 h, followed by monocytes influx peaking at 12-24 h, both exacerbating secondary neuronal death and infarct expansion38–40. Our drug-loaded dual-stiffness NPs were designed to break this vicious cycle by enabling compartment-specific therapeutic precision guided by spatial pathology.

We constructed an in vitro ischemic stroke BBB model to verify the compartment-specific therapeutic effects. Primary isolated neutrophils were utilized to mimic peripheral blood immune cells, with fMLP factor supplementation inducing inflammatory responses. An in vitro damaged BBB model was established by seeding endothelial cells in the upper chamber and PC12 neuronal cells in the lower chamber with oxygen-glucose deprivation/reperfusion (OGD/R) applied. This simulated post-ischemic stroke peripheral inflammation and central neural damage (Fig. 5e). Four groups were designed: Group A (dual-stiffness NPs: Pic@stiff + NBP@soft), Group B (single-soft NPs: Pic@soft + NBP@soft), Group C (single-stiff NPs: Pic@stiff + NBP@stiff), and Group D (no treatment). Although NPs with different stiffness can suppress neutrophils transmigration to the lower chamber and protect damaged neural cells, there were significant differences among these groups. In contrast to Group A, Group B (single-soft NPs) showed minimal ability to suppress neutrophils transmigration to the lower chamber. This deficiency exacerbated PC12 cell damage under high-inflammatory conditions, underscoring the necessity of stiff NPs to achieve robust immune cell uptake and anti-inflammatory in the upper chamber. Conversely, Group C (single-stiff NPs) exhibited substantial immune-mediated NPs clearance in the upper chamber, effectively limiting neutrophils infiltration. However, the poor penetration of stiff NPs resulted in inferior PC12 cell survival compared to Group A. This highlights the critical role of the soft NPs in bypassing upper-chamber clearance to deliver neurorestorative agents to PC12 cells (Fig. 5f, g).

Building on the findings in Fig. 3 regarding the spatially distinct uptake patterns of dual-stiffness NPs, we hypothesize that the therapeutic advantage of Group A arises from the following mechanism: (i) Pic@stiff is preferentially internalized by immune cells in the upper-chamber, releasing Pic to suppress inflammation-induced neutrophils activation and subsequent transmigration across the BBB; (ii) NBP@soft, protected by stiff NPs to evade immune surveillance, migrates to the lower chamber where they are internalized by PC12 neuronal cells, triggering localized NBP release to promote neuronal recovery. This dual-stiffness strategy enables simultaneous spatially targeted treatment of peripheral anti-inflammatory and central neuroprotective through a single administration.

We further evaluated the biodistribution of the drug-loaded dual-stiffness NPs in MCAO/R mice. The in vivo results demonstrated that Pic@stiff significantly increased their hepatic retention and decreased brain accumulation (Fig. 5h~k). Meanwhile, compared to the drug-free biodistribution (Fig. 4d, e), this drug-loaded dual-stiffness NPs strategy protected NBP@soft from peripheral immune clearance, reducing their hepatic accumulation while markedly improving brain delivery. These findings might result from Pic@stiff releasing Pic following internalization by peripheral immune cell, thereby suppressing immunity activation, while NBP@soft evaded immune clearance under protection, leading to significantly enhanced brain accumulation. This reaffirms that co-administration of drug-loaded stiff NPs and soft NPs enhances their distribution in peripheral and brain compartments, respectively, achieving synergistic dual-compartments therapy for ischemic stroke.

Peripheral immune suppression of drug-loaded dual-stiffness NPs
To validate the peripheral immune suppression of dual-stiffness NPs, we next examined the expression level of the immune cell migration-related protein CD18 and quantified immune cell retention in the brain during the acute phase of ischemic stroke (Fig. 6a). Our experimental results demonstrated that Groups A, B, and C all reduced CD18 expression (Fig. 6b, c). Notably, Group A (dual-stiffness NPs) and Group C (single-stiff NPs) exhibited significantly greater efficacy in suppressing CD18 expression in monocytes compared to Group B (single-soft NPs), beneficial for inhibiting immune cell migration into the ischemic hemisphere (Fig. 6d, e). While the inhibition effect of Group C was significantly weaker than that of Group A, analysis of the contralateral hemisphere using the same methods revealed minimal immune cell infiltration (1-3% of total cells), consistent with the acute phase of stroke (Supplementary Fig. 14). Group A still effectively reduced contralateral immune cell infiltration compared to untreated controls, suggesting a protective effect against secondary brain damage.

Massive immune cell infiltration during stroke promotes the release of tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), which disrupts the BBB and induces adhesion molecule expression, further facilitating leukocyte migration. Concurrently, the extensive immune cell infiltration leads to the reactivation of inflammation in ischemic regions, subsequently activating microglia in the brain to release interleukin-1β (IL-1β). This cytokine promotes massive immune cell infiltration into brain tissue through the CXCL1/2 pathway, amplifying inflammatory responses and further compromising BBB integrity by increasing permeability. In early-stage ischemic stroke, Group A and Group C significantly reduced peripheral immune cell infiltration into the brain. When examining inflammatory cytokine levels in the lesioned brain hemisphere of MCAO/R mice on Day 1 of treatment, Group A showed a significant reduction in TNF-α levels and demonstrated a downward trend in IL-1β. Group C also exhibited significant reductions in both TNF-α and IL-1β levels during the early phase, indicating that the superior inhibition of Pic@stiff for immune cell infiltration into brain tissue facilitates early-phase inflammation control (Fig. 6f).

Group A maintained suppression of immune cell migration through Day 3, whereas other groups lacked sustained efficacy. By Day 3, Group A exhibited minimal neutrophil signals, confirming the efficacy of the dual-stiffness NPs combination in suppressing peripheral neutrophil recruitment via Pic@stiff (Supplementary Fig. 15a), consistent with Fig. 6d. Notably, either single stiff or soft NPs therapy reduced fluorescence signals compared to Group D but remained suboptimal, highlighting the necessity of combining NPs of differing stiffness to enhance peripheral immune cell uptake. Meanwhile, ICAM-1, a vascular endothelial adhesion molecule, exhibits upregulated expression post-stroke, peaking at 24-72 h before gradual decline. We evaluated ICAM-1 levels in the ipsilateral brain at Day 3, observing significant downregulation in Group A compared to the others (Fig. 6g). This indicates that the therapeutic approach of Group A effectively suppressed immune cell infiltration into brain tissue via the integrin-vascular endothelial adhesion molecule pathway, while single-stiffness NP Groups B and C failed to demonstrate such inhibition.

Central microenvironment regulation of drug-loaded dual-stiffness NPs
We next investigated the regulation of the central microenvironment following the administration of drug-loaded dual-stiffness NPs. To evaluate the modulatory effect of NBP@soft within this system on the ischemic microenvironment and its neuroprotective potential, key parameters in the ischemic hemisphere were assessed, including immune cell infiltration factors, brain inflammatory cytokines, BBB restoration, cerebral edema severity, infarct volume, and neural injury biomarkers. In Group A (dual-stiffness NPs), Pic@stiff shielded NBP@soft from peripheral clearance, thereby facilitating NBP delivery to neuronal cells and modulating the local microenvironment. As a result, the level of MPO, NE, and pro-inflammatory cytokines TNF-α and IL-1β were significantly reduced on Day 3 post-treatment. Group B (single-soft NPs) also exhibited reduced inflammatory burden, particularly in IL-1β suppression. In contrast, Group C (single-stiff NPs) showed cytokine levels that rebounded to near untreated levels, indicating that while stiff NPs initially inhibited peripheral immune infiltration, the absence of soft NPs compromised sustained neuroprotection and failed to remodel the pathological microenvironment, limiting their therapeutic durability in the MCAO/R model (Fig. 7a, b).

Persistent activation of immune cells and accumulation of inflammatory factors will exacerbate BBB disruption. In the untreated Group D, extensive dextran leakage and dense perilesional aggregates were observed, along with a pronounced decrease in Occludin expression—a tight junction protein essential for BBB integrity—indicating severe barrier disruption. In contrast, Group A exhibited minimal dextran deposition with only sparse isolated puncta, even within the infarct core (Supplementary Fig. 15b). Occludin level in Group A was restored to close to Sham values, effectively mitigating injury-induced BBB hyperpermeability (Fig. 7c). These results indicated that dual-stiffness NPs achieved timely modulation of the cerebral pathological microenvironment, significantly attenuating BBB permeability and suppressing degradation of tight junction proteins.

Moreover, Group A also restrained the expansion of edema and limited infarct progression. On Day 3 post-treatment, brain water content in Group A was significantly reduced (78.33 ± 0.36%) compared to controls (80.54 ± 0.67%, p < 0.0001), and infarct volume was markedly decreased (6.52 ± 4.21% vs. 48.73 ± 19.11% in controls, p < 0.0001). In contrast, Groups B and C, lacking spatial stage-selective delivery capacity during the acute phase, showed elevated edema and larger infarcts versus Group A (Fig. 7d, e).

Further assessment of neural cell recovery was performed on Day 3 post-treatment using TUNEL staining to label damaged neural cells. The TUNEL signal in brain tissue sections was significantly lower in Groups A and B compared to Groups C and D, indicating that the administration methods in experimental Groups A and B facilitated post-stroke neuronal recovery (Fig. 7f). This also underscores the critical importance of drug delivery via soft NPs in neuroprotection. These results demonstrated that combining drug-loaded NPs of varying stiffness—employing stiff NPs to rapidly suppress peripheral inflammatory storms while enabling soft NPs to deliver neuroprotective agents to the central environment under protection.

Therapeutic effect of drug-loaded dual-stiffness NPs in MCAO/R mice
We confirmed that drug-loaded dual-stiffness NPs achieved sustained peripheral anti-inflammatory and central microenvironment regulation through a single administration. Based on this finding, we applied this treatment strategy to MCAO/R mice over a 28-day period.

After inducing MCAO/R in mice, neurological severity was assessed using the modified Neurological Severity Score (mNSS), including sensory, motor, balance, reflex, and limb flexion parameters. Mice with mNSS >10 were randomized into groups and administered treatments according to the timeline in Fig. 8a. Survival rates, body weight changes, and mNSS scores were tracked from treatment initiation to Day 28.

The combined peripheral anti-inflammatory effect of stiff NPs and the central neuroprotective action of soft NPs synergistically enhanced survival rates and promoted neurological recovery in MCAO/R mice. The results showed that the drug- loaded dual-stiffness NPs (Group A) achieved the highest survival rate (77.8%), significantly surpassing the untreated group (11.1%, Fig. 8b). Group A maintained stable body weight starting from Day 2, while other groups exhibited continuous weight loss over the initial 3 days (Fig. 8c). It also significantly reduced mNSS scores in the early phase compared to untreated controls (Fig. 8d), demonstrating early neurofunctional improvement. Remarkably, Group A rescued severely injured mice and achieved uniformly low final mNSS scores during the long-term treatment period (Fig. 8e, f).

For Group B treated with single-soft NPs alone, the survival rate was only 22.2%. Due to the absence of stiff NPs to promptly suppress inflammation during the early phase, Group B mice exhibited substantial mortality in the first 4 days (Fig. 8b). Group B mice with high mNSS scores on Day 0 (indicating severe injury) did not survive post-treatment, while the two surviving mice showed significantly lower final mNSS scores and enhanced neurological recovery (Fig. 8e~g). Combined with Section before, this outcome may arise from the failure of soft NPs to rapidly suppress peripheral inflammation during the acute phase of ischemic stroke. In severe injury cases, intense ischemia-induced inflammation overwhelmed the delayed anti-inflammatory action of Group B's NPs, resulting in therapeutic failure and high mortality. Group C treated with single-stiff NPs showed higher survival rates than Group B. However, survivors retained elevated mNSS scores at the endpoint, indicating poor neurological recovery (e.g., persistent beam balance deficits and severe limb flexion). This might be attributed to stiff NPs predominantly exerting early-phase anti-inflammatory effects, while lacking sustained neuroprotective capabilities essential for long-term recovery.

To validate our interpretations and isolate the contribution of NPs delivery versus drug synergy, we conducted long-term control treatment experiments with five designed control groups (Supplementary Fig. 17, 18): Group E (only-soft NPs: NBP@soft), Group F (only-stiff NPs: Pic@stiff), Group G (dual-stiffness NPs without drug: stiff NPs and soft NPs without loading drug), Group H (drug-swapped dual-stiffness NPs: NBP@stiff + Pic@soft), Group I (free drug without NPs: NBP and Pic) and a Sham Group. Our results demonstrated all of the control treatment experiments showed lower survival rates and worse mNSS scores on Day 28 compared to the final formulation Group A. Group E showed high early-phase mortality, particularly among severely injured animals, indicating failure to provide acute protection. Groups F, G, and H, each containing stiff NPs, modestly delayed early mortality, likely through transient peripheral inflammation suppression via phagocytosis, but lacked durable neuroprotection. In assessing neurological functional recovery, drug-free Group G exhibited an average score of 10 on the mNSS at 28 days, indicating minimal neural repair. Group F which contained Pic@stiff retained high mNSS scores. In contrast, Group E utilized NBP@soft achieving significant attenuation of neurological deficits in surviving mice. As to Group H, swapped drug in dual-stiffness NPs system showed diminished survival rates and failed to rescue profoundly affected subjects, emphasizing the importance of compartment-specific drug allocation. And the free drug group (Group I) performed a survival rate of only 11.1%, likely due to rapid systemic clearance and minimal brain accumulation. These results demonstrated the therapeutic superiority of our stiffness-tiered drug delivery strategy - Pic-loaded stiff NPs combined with NBP-loaded soft NPs.

Neuronal recovery of drug-loaded dual-stiffness NPs in MCAO/R mice
To quantify neuronal recovery, brain tissue sections were stained and analyzed to assess neuronal status, population, and morphology (Fig. 8h). In Group D, Nissl bodies of untreated MCAO/R mice were significantly reduced with dissolution and fragmentation in the infarcted areas, indicating widespread neuronal damage. The mice in Group A substantially improved neuronal organization in the hippocampal region and increased Nissl body density with restored structural integrity, suggesting functional neuronal recovery. Surviving mice in Group B demonstrated comparable neurorestorative outcomes to Group A. In contrast, Group C exhibited minimal neuronal recovery, which aligns with their elevated mNSS observed in Fig. 8e. Neurofilament immunostaining revealed discontinuous and shrink fibers, and punctate aggregates with reduced density in Group D. In contrast, Groups A and B exhibited preserved filamentous structures and high positive signals. GFAP analysis demonstrated pronounced astrogliosis and scar formation in Groups C and D, whereas Groups A and B showed attenuated glial scarring and diminished apoptotic neuron signals in lesioned areas.

In summary, the dual-stiffness NPs delivery system synergistically addressed acute inflammation (via stiff NPs) and long-term neural repair (via soft NPs), significantly improving survival and functional recovery in ischemic stroke. This therapeutic regimen also demonstrated a favorable safety profile (Supplementary Fig. 19).

Synthesis and characterization of nanoparticles
To prepare PLGA NPs, 80 mg of PLGA was dissolved in 5 mL of acetone solution and ultrasonically dissolved as the oil phase. For the aqueous phase: ultrapure water was heated on a magnetic stirrer, and polyvinyl alcohol (P VA, 0.2%) was added while stirring. After complete dissolution, the oil phase was slowly added to the aqueous phase, stirred for about 30 min, transferred to an eggplant-shaped flask, and the organic solvent was evaporated under reduced pressure at 40 °C, 0.08 MPa for 1.5 h to obtain a PLGA NPs suspension. To prepare Lipo-PLGA NPs, the PLGA NPs suspension was filtered through a 0.8 μm membrane. Microfluidics was used to coat lipids onto the surface of PLGA. Based on preliminary experimental screening, the condition of microfluidic preparation method was: PLGA: lipid (mass ratio) = 4:1, aqueous phase: organic phase volume = 1:1, flow rate = 12 mL/min. The organic solvent was removed by overnight stirring. Confocal microscopy was used to examine the complete encapsulation of liposomes on the surface of PLGA, forming Lipo-PLGA. Anionic liposomes were prepared using the thin-film ultrasonic method. Certain amount of phosphatidylserine and soybean lecithin were mixed and dissolved in chloroform. Then chloroform was evaporated under reduced pressure using a rotary evaporator, followed by placement in a vacuum desiccator for 2 h to ensure complete removal of residual chloroform. After drying, 5 mL of dispersion medium was added to swell and hydrate the film. The mixture was then placed in an ultrasonic cleaner for bath sonication for 15 minutes, followed by transfer to an EP tube and probe sonication for 3 minutes to complete the preparation.

The particle size and zeta potential of the NPs were measured using a Malvern particle size and zeta potential analyzer (DLS). The morphology of the NPs was observed using transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and the Young's modulus and surface topography of the NPs were determined using atomic force microscopy (AFM). In this study, Lipo-PLGA and Liposome were designed as stiff NPs and soft NPs model respectively.

Cellular uptake pathways of NPs with different stiffness
Different endocytic inhibitors were utilized to investigate whether the pathways of NPs with similar size, zeta potential, and surface morphology but varying stiffness enter immune cells are consistent. Raw264.7 cells were selected as the cellular model for the experiment, seeded in 24-well plates at a density of 105 cells per well. Three endocytic inhibitors were chosen for the study: EIPA (inhibits macropinocytosis and phagocytosis, 10 μM), genistein (inhibits caveolae-mediated endocytosis, 10 μM), and chlorpromazine (inhibits clathrin-mediated endocytosis, 30 μM). After co-incubated with the cells for 30 min, 1 mg/mL Lipo-PLGA (DiD-labeled, 1:1000) and 1 mg/mL Liposome (DiD-labeled, 1:1000) were administered separately, followed by a 2 h co-incubation. Flow cytometry was then used to analyze the percentage of cellular uptake and the mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) within the cells.

Different cell lines uptake NPs with different stiffness
To determine the uptake kinetics of NPs with different stiffness levels by immune cells, this study utilized Raw264.7 cells as the cellular model. Raw264.7 cells (105 cells per well) were seeded in plates. 1 mg/mL of Lipo-PLGA (DiI-labeled, 1:1000) and Liposome (DiI-labeled, 1:1000) were administered at 100 μL per well, respectively. The cells were co-incubated with the NPs at 37°C for 1, 2, 3, and 4 h. After incubation, cells were detached using a cell scraper, collected and processed for flow cytometry analysis to compare the MFI within Raw264.7 cells at different time points, reflecting the differential uptake rates of stiff NPs and soft NPs. 2 h was selected as the timepoint to quantify the uptake of different stiffness NPs by different cell types. This experiment employed BV2 microglial cells and PC12 neuronal cells as in vitro models. Cells were seeded at a density of 105 cells per well in 24-well plates and cultured overnight. The next day, 100 μL of Lipo-PLGA and Liposome, at identical concentrations and dosages as above, were administered to the cells. After 2 h of incubation at 37°C, cells were gently collected into flow cytometry tubes. Post-processing flow cytometry was performed to compare the MFI of each NPs type across the two cell lines. The gating strategy was implemented as follows: Initial identification of cells was performed using a FSC-A versus SSC-A plotto exclude cell debris. To ensure data reflected individual cellular uptake rather than aggregates, singlets were gated using an FSC-A versus FSC-H plot. Only the linear population was retained for downstream analysis. The cellular uptake was quantified by measuring the MFI and the percentage of DiI-positive cells in the PE channel. For each sample, a minimum of 10,000 total events were collected. Data were processed using FlowJo software. Background fluorescence was determined using untreated cells as a negative control to set the threshold for DiI-positive populations.

Distribution of dual stiffness NP combination in vitro
Primary neutrophils were extracted from C57BL/6 mice. The mice were euthanized by cervical dislocation and sterilized by immersion in 75% alcohol for 5 min. The leg bones of the mice were removed, sterilized, and the primary cells from the bone marrow were flushed out using a syringe. The cell suspension was passed through a 40 μm cell strainer, and the liquid was centrifuged at 510 g for 5 min to collect the primary cells. Red blood cell (RBC) lysis buffer was used to remove RBCs from the primary cells. A density gradient centrifugation tube with gradients of 78%, 65%, and 55% was prepared using Percoll separation medium and NaCl solution. The primary cells were added to the tube and centrifuged at 1,780 g for 30 min. Cells collected at the interface between 78%-65% and the middle of 55% were considered primary neutrophils. These cells were resuspended in serum-containing culture medium for subsequent experiments.

In a Transwell plate (24-well, 8 μm), neutrophils were added to the upper chamber (2 × 105, 200 μL per well), while PC12 cells (105 cells, 1mL per well) were pre-seeded in the lower chamber. Fluorescently labeled NPs combination carriers of different stiffnesses were added to the upper chamber. After 2 h, the penetration into the lower chamber and uptake by PC12 cells, as well as the phagocytosis of NPs by neutrophils in the upper chamber, were examined. The gating strategy for flow cytometry analysis of neutrophils and PC12 cells was consistent with the procedures described in the “Different cell lines uptake NPs with different stiffness” section.

Mesoscopic model of nanoparticle endocytosis
The endocytosis of nanoparticles by cellular membranes was simulated based on a coarse-grained molecular dynamics (CGMD) method. The phospholipid membrane system used a three-bead solvent-free model that was developed by Cooke et al.44 In this model, the phospholipid molecules exhibit a three-particle form that consists of one hydrophilic head particle and two hydrophobic tail particles. The molecular structure is maintained by finite extension nonlinear elastic (FENE) bonds, given by,

where 𝑘 represents the spring stiffness and 𝑅 denotes the maximum range of the bond. In this work, 𝑘 is set to 3𝜖/𝜎2 and 𝑅 is set to 1.5𝜎 . This configuration enables the controlled extensibility of the chain.

An approximate unit system has been adopted for the CGMD simulations, where unit length and unit time are defined as 𝜎 and 𝜏, respectively, corresponding to physical values of 1 nm and 7.7 ns. Thermal energy has been maintained at 𝑘 𝑇 = 1.1𝜖, with the energy unit 𝜖 being equivalent to 3.89×10−21 J. All simulated particles have been assigned a diameter of 1.0𝜎 (1 nm).

The bilayer membrane contains 45,000 phospholipid molecules, constituting a 158×158𝜎2 planar structure with periodic boundary conditions. The planar membrane extends along the 𝑥 and 𝑦 directions, possessing a relative size sufficient to allow complete internalization under appropriate conditions. Free energy calculations
To elucidate the superior uptake efficiency of stiff NP over soft NP from an energetic perspective, we computed the Gibbs free energy change during phagocytosis in the NPT ensemble using the steered molecular dynamics (SMD) module in LPAMMPS. In this setup, a harmonic spring linking a virtual particle to the NP pulled the latter towards the membrane interior at a constant velocity. The pulling speed was set low enough to approximate a quasi-static, reversible process. The free energy was evaluated using Jarzynski’s equality:
𝛥𝐹 = −𝛽−1 ln〈𝑒−𝛽𝑊〉 (5)
where 𝛥𝐹 = 𝐹𝐵 −𝐹𝐴 denote the free energy difference between the initial state A and the final state B, W is the work performed along the pulling trajectory, and 𝛽 = (𝑘 𝑇)−1. This identity rigorously connects non-equilibrium work statistics to equilibrium free energy differences in the limit of infinitely slow perturbation.

Observation of actin distribution in different cell types
Raw264.7 cells and PC12 cells were seeded into confocal dishes at a density of 105 cells per well. On the following day, cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 10 min and washed three times with PBS. The actin cytoskeleton was stained with Actin-Tracker (1:200 dilution) for 30 min at room temperature, followed by two PBS washes. Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI for 10 min, washed twice with PBS, and covered with 500 µL PBS to keep cells hydrated and prevent detachment. Actin organization and distribution in both cell types were observed under a laser scanning confocal microscope under identical staining and imaging conditions.

Actin inhibited experiments
To inhibit actin dynamics and evaluate its role in NP uptake, cytochalasin D (CytD) was used. Raw264.7 cells and PC12 cells were seeded in 24-well plates at a density of 105 cells per well. On the following day, the culture medium was replaced with fresh medium containing CytD at final concentrations of 2 µM, 1 µM, 0.5 µM, or 0 µM (sterilized using a 0.22 µm filter). Raw264.7 cells were incubated with CytD for 12 h, while PC12 cells, being more fragile, were treated for only 4 h. After incubation, the medium was replaced with normal culture medium. Subsequently, 1 mg/mL of stiff NPs (DiD-labeled, 1:1000) and soft NPs (DiD-labeled, 1:1000) were added to each well (100 µL per well, respectively). After 2 h of incubation at 37°C, cells were gently harvested into flow cytometry tubes. Flow cytometry analysis was performed to compare the MFI of each NP type between the two cell lines.

Decoupling of cellular uptake stages
To separate the binding and internalization stages of NP uptake, temperature-controlled experiments were conducted. Raw264.7 cells and PC12 cells were seeded in 24-well plates at a density of 105 cells per well. On the following day, the medium was replaced with pre-cooled cultura medium, and the cells were incubated at 4°C for 1 h. Stiff NPs (DiD-labeled, 1:1000) and soft NPs (DiD-labeled, 1:1000) were then added at a concentration of 1 mg/mL (100 µL per well, respectively). The cells were maintained at 4°C for 1.5 h to allow sufficient NP binding, followed by incubation at 37°C for 3 h to enable internalization. Cells were subsequently collected into flow cytometry tubes, and the MFI was measured to quantify NP uptake.

Variation in the distribution of nanoparticles (NPs) with different stiffness in the bloodstream of MCAO/R mice following administration of dual-stiffness NPs
MCAO/R mouse model was constructed. Mice were anesthetized with 1% sodium pentobarbital and fixed in a supine position. Exposing the left external carotid artery (ECA) and internal carotid artery (ICA). A suture with a tip diameter of 0.23 ± 0.01 mm was inserted from the ECA into the ICA until significant resistance was encountered, blocking the blood flow of the middle cerebral artery (MCA). The wound was then sutured, and the mice were transferred to a 37 °C incubator to maintain body temperature. After 1 h, the suture was withdrawn to restore collateral circulation, initiating the reperfusion phase.

Within 6 h post-modeling, a combination of stiff NPs (DiO-labeled, 1:200) and soft NPs (DiO-labeled, 1:200) was administered intravenously to explore the distribution of NPs with different stiffnesses in the blood circulation of MCAO/R mice. At 5 min post-administration, 100 μL of peripheral blood was collected via the orbital sinus. The whole blood was centrifuged at 300 g for 5 min. The supernatant was discarded, and 1 mL of RBC lysis buffer was added to the pellet for 10 min of lysis. After lysis, adding equal volume of HBSS to terminate lysis, the sample was centrifuged at 300 g for 5 min, and the cell pellet was resuspended in 1 mL of HBSS (on ice). The sample was centrifuged again at 300 g for 5 min to wash away the lysis buffer. This step was repeated once. Antibody staining solution was prepared. Each million cells were treated with 0.2 μg of antibody. The cell pellet was resuspended in 80 μL of the mixed antibody staining solution, and an equivalent amount of Fc blocker was added. After incubating for 45 min, the free staining solution was washed away, and flow cytometry analysis was performed. Initial events were gated on FSC-A versus SSC-A and FSC-H versus FSC-A plots to identify the main cell population and ensure singlet discrimination, consistent with the procedures described in the section before. Within the singlet gate, CD45+ (PE/Cy7) events were identified as the total leukocyte population to exclude residual RBC debris and non-immune events. From the CD45+ parent gate, neutrophils were further identified as the CD11b+ (APC) and Ly6G+ (PerCP/Cy5.5) double-positive population. NP uptake was then quantified by measuring the MFI of DiO (FITC channel) within these specific subsets. Data were analyzed using FlowJo software.

Due to the low proportion of immune cells in whole blood, the number of immune cells with NPs signals observed in the mentioned experimental method was very limited. Therefore, further experiments combining in vivo and in vitro approaches were conducted to measure changes in the distribution of NPs with different stiffnesses in the blood circulation after combination administration. Specifically, blood was collected from the orbital sinus of mice 6 h post-modeling, and RBC lysis was performed following the steps described above. Leukocytes were isolated from the peripheral blood of the mice, resuspended in 2 mL of HBSS solution. The cells were then co-incubated with the stiff NPs and soft NPs in vitro for 1 h (at 37°C, 100 rpm on a shaker). Following the same steps as before, the cells were stained and labeled, and flow cytometry was used to investigate changes in the uptake of NPs with different stiffnesses under the soft and stiff combination drug delivery mode.

Formation and separation of the protein corona of NPs
Peripheral blood was collected from C57BL/6 mice via retro-orbital bleeding (1.5 mL per mouse) into Eppendorf tubes and allowed to clot for 1 h at room temperature. The samples were centrifuged at 2,810 g for 10 min, and the supernatant serum was collected. The obtained serum was diluted with saline at a 1:1 ratio to prepare 50% serum. This diluted serum was incubated with stiff or soft NPs for 2 h, followed by centrifugation at 20,000 g for 45 min. The supernatant was discarded, and the NP pellets were resuspended in 1 mL PBS to obtain NP suspensions coated with their respective protein coronas.

To evaluate how the combination of stiff and soft NPs influences the composition of each NP’s protein corona, a sequential serum preconditioning strategy was employed.

Taking stiff NPs as an example, peripheral blood was collected from C57BL/6 mice (1.5 mL via retro-orbital bleeding) and allowed to clot for 1 h. Soft NPs were added to the serum and incubated for 1 h to simulate their in vivo exposure, followed by centrifugation to remove the NPs. The resulting “soft NP–pretreated” serum was diluted with saline (1:1) to obtain 50% serum and subsequently incubated with stiff NPs for 2 h. After incubation, the mixture was centrifuged for 45 min at 20,000 g, the supernatant was discarded, and the pellet was resuspended in 1 mL PBS to obtain stiff NPs with adsorbed protein coronas. The same procedure was performed in reverse (preincubating serum with stiff NPs before adding soft NPs) to analyze protein corona composition changes on soft NPs.

Processing and analysis of protein corona samples
Protein Extraction and Digestion
Frozen NP–protein corona samples were thawed on ice and lysed in 8 M urea buffer containing 1% PMSF and 2 mM EDTA. Proteins were reduced with 10 mM DTT at 37°C for 1 h and alkylated with 22 mM iodoacetamide in the dark for 15 min at room temperature. After dilution with 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate, proteins were digested sequentially with trypsin and Lys-C at 37°C for 2 h. The reaction was stopped by acidifying the mixture to pH 2–3 with 20% TFA. Peptides were desalted using C18 cartridges (Millipore, Billerica, MA, USA) and quantified with the Pierce™ Quantitative Peptide Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific).

LC–MS/MS Analysis
Peptide samples were analyzed using a Vanquish Neo UHPLC system (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Mobile phase A consisted of 0.1% formic acid in water, and mobile phase B was acetonitrile with 0.1% formic acid. Peptides were separated using a trap-and-elute dual-column setup, with a PepMap Neo Trap Cartridge (300 µm × 5 mm, 5 µm) and an Easy-Spray™ PepMap™ Neo UHPLC analytical column (150 µm × 15 cm, 2 µm). The column temperature was maintained at 55°C with a flow rate of 2.5 µL/min.

Mass Spectrometry Detection
Data-independent acquisition (DIA) was performed on an Orbitrap Astral high-resolution mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) in positive ion mode. Full MS scans were acquired from 380–980 m/z at a resolution of 240,000 (at 200 m/z), with an AGC target of 500% and a maximum injection time of 5 ms. MS2 scans were acquired with DIA mode using 299 variable windows (2 Th), a normalized collision energy of 25%, and a resolution of 120,000.

Database search and quantification
Raw DIA data were analyzed using DIA-NN (v1.8.1) in library-free mode against the UniProtKB Mus musculus reference proteome (UP000000589, 54,910 sequences). Spectral libraries were generated using deep-learning prediction and refined with the MBR (Match Between Runs) function. The false discovery rate (FDR) was controlled below 1% at both precursor and protein levels. Quantitative data from validated identifications were used for downstream analysis.

The preparation process involved removing the brainstem and cerebellum, dividing the brain into left and right hemispheres. The tissue was then minced and passed through a cell strainer. The myelin layer and supernatant were carefully aspirated, leaving the cell pellet at the bottom of the tube. The pellet was resuspended in 10 mL of HBSS, transferred to a new 15 mL tube, and centrifuged (286 g, 5 min, 10 °C). Initial gates were set on FSC-A/SSC-A and FSC-A/FSC-H to exclude cell debris and doublets. Within the singlet gate, a primary gate was set on CD11b+ (APC) events to identify the total myeloid cell population. The protein concentration was determined using a BCA kit, and the inflammatory levels in the lesioned brain side of mice from different experimental groups were compared on the 1st and 3rd days after treatment.

Brain tissue sections staining
After long-term treatment, coronal brain sections (4-6 µm thickness) were prepared. For Nissl staining, sections were immersed in staining solution at 50°C for 30 minutes, rinsed twice with 70% ethanol, and mounted with neutral resin. Immunofluorescence staining involved overnight incubation at 4°C with primary antibodies (anti-neurofilament, anti-GFAP), followed by species-matched secondary antibodies (Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG). All sections were imaged using an Olympus VS200 digital slide scanner.

BBB permeability assessment
On the 3rd day after drug administration, the mice were anesthetized, and their brains were perfused with PBS and extracted. The brain tissues were processed according to the method described aboved. The expression of Occludin, a protein associated with tight junctions of the BBB, was measured using WB analysis. The full scan blots are provided in Source Data file.

3 days after drug administration, the permeability of the BBB was investigated using TRITC-labeled dextran (TRITC-Dextran). The dextran (2 μg, 200 μL/20 g) was intravenously injected and circulated in the mice for 2 h. Afterward, the brains were perfused with PBS and extracted intact. The extracted brain tissues were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde, embedded in paraffin, and sectioned coronally at a thickness of 4-6 μm to facilitate observation of the cortical and hippocampal regions. Following dewaxing, the sections were stained with 10 μg/mL DAPI and mounted. The sections were then scanned using a virtual digital slide scanning system.

Cerebral edema content
The extent of brain tissue edema was assessed using the dry-wet weight method. On the 3rd day after drug administration, mice were anesthetized and subjected to cardiac perfusion with PBS. The brain tissue was then weighed and recorded as W wet. After freeze-drying (pre-frozen at -80 °C overnight and then lyophilized for 48 h), the tissue was weighed again and recorded as W dry. The percentage water content in the brain tissue of each group of mice was determined using formula:
Cerebral edema content(%) = (W wet −W dry) ×100% (8)
W wet

Cerebral infarction volume.
On the 3rd day following MCAO/R treatment, the mice were anesthetized and subjected to cardiac perfusion with PBS. The brain tissue was carefully extracted and stored at -20 °C for 1 h. Once the brain tissue was frozen solid, it was sliced coronally into approximately 2 mm-thick sections, yielding 5 uniform slices. The brain slices were immersed in a 1.5% solution of TTC and incubated at 37 °C, 30 min. After staining, each slice was divided along the midline into the infarcted hemisphere and the contralateral hemisphere, which were separately weighed and recorded as W infarcted and W contralateral. The brain tissue was then soaked in 3 mL of freshly prepared TTC extraction solution (anhydrous ethanol: DMSO = 1:1, v/v) and kept in the dark. After 24 h, the extraction solution was replaced with 3 mL of fresh solution, and the tissue was soaked for an additional 24 h in the dark. The two extraction solutions were combined, mixed thoroughly, and the absorbance at 490 nm was measured using a microplate reader, recorded as A infarcted and A contralateral. The percentage volume of the cerebral infarction was calculated using formula:
Cerebral infarction volume(%) = (1− A infarcted × W contralateral )×100% (9)
A contralateral × W infarcted

Long-term treatment experiment
Following the method outlined before, the mice were subjected to modeling, and drug administration. The survival status and behavior of the MCAO/R mice were meticulously recorded and assessed over a 28-day treatment period. By comparing survival rates, weight recovery, mNSS scores, the therapeutic efficacy of the dual-stiffness NPs administration on MCAO/R mice was investigated, along with the recovery of impaired neurological functions.

Safety evaluation
After long-term treatment, coronal brain sections (4-6 µm thickness) were prepared for H&E staining. Sections were imaged using an Olympus VS200 digital slide scanner.

Statistical analysis
All statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 10.4.1 software (USA). Data are expressed as mean ± SD. For comparisons between two groups, an unpaired two-tailed t-test was used. For comparisons among multiple groups with a single variable, one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s multiple comparison post-hoc test was performed. For comparisons among multiple groups involving two independent variables, two-way ANOVA followed by Sidak’s multiple comparison post-hoc test was performed. For measurements of recovery scores over the 28-day period, a two-way ANOVA (or mixed-effects model) was conducted using the Compare column means (main column effect) approach to assess overall treatment effects across time. To further investigate the time-specific differences, a two-way ANOVA (or mixed-effect model) with simple effects within rows was applied to compare the groups at each individual time point. Statistical significance was determined based on the calculated p-values.

Data Availability
The mass spectrometry proteomics data generated in this study have been deposited to the iProX database with the dataset identifier IPX0015471000. All data generated or analyzed during this study are included in this published article and its Supplementary Information files. The source data underlying all main figures (Figs. 2–8) and supplementary figures are provided with the paper as a Source Data file.

Code Availability
Data collection was performed using the open-source software LAMMPS (version 30 July 2016; https://lammps.sandia.gov). All simulation parameters, force fields, and boundary conditions required to reproduce the results are fully described in the Methods section. Data analysis and visualization were conducted using OVITO (version 3.4.4; https://www.ovito.org).

2. For the dual-stiffness NPs drug delivery system, the stiff NP were designed to carry Pic and the soft NP were designed to carry NBP. What are the differences in drug release of NP with different stiffness?
Thank you very much for your questions. In general, the drug release behavior of NPs is primarily determined by the NPs compositions, structure, and the interaction between the drug and NPs. Stiffness has not been demonstrated to directely alter the physicochemical drug release kinetics of NPs in current studies. Instead, stiffness mainly affects the biological fate of NPs, such as barrier penetration ability, recoginition and uptake by immune cells, and circulation time, which in the end exerts indirect influences on the overall pharmacodynamic performance.
Our design was guided by the biodistribution tendencies of the stiff and soft NPs. In the dual-stiffness NP system, the stiff Lipo-PLGA NPs prefer to be more efficiently taken up by peripheral immune cells, while the soft Liposome NPs, being less recognized by the immune system, can passively accumulate in the brain.
Accordingly, stiff NPs were designed to carry Piceatannol (Pic), a Syk kinase inhibitor (a key regulator of integrin signaling) to downregulate integrin β2 expression and suppress leukocyte adhesion, migration. Pic@stiff NPs achieved immune modulation in the peripheral compartment, where stiff NPs were predominantly distributed and internalized. Meanwhile, NBP, a clinically approved neuroprotective drug for ischemic stroke, was encapsulated in the soft NPs, enabling enhanced brain delivery and exertion of antioxidant and neuroprotective effects within the CNS.
This drug design aligns the pharmacological action of the drug with the spatial delivery behavior of NPs with different stiffness, realizing a rational dual-space therapeutic strategy.
In our system, the two types of NPs differ in their main material composition—PLGA for the stiff NPs and lipid bilayers for the soft ones—so the drug release profiles are primarily governed by the physicochemical properties of these materials rather than stiffness itself.
In response to this comment, the drug release data has been included and revisions have been made as follow:
CD18 (integrin β2), a critical subunit of functional integrins LFA-1 and Mac-132, mediates the binding of peripheral immune cells to vascular endothelial adhesion molecules (e.g., ICAM-1) under ischemic stroke conditions33, promoting massive infiltration of neutrophils, monocytes, and other leukocytes into the brain. The stiff NPs were designed to carry Pic34, a Syk kinase inhibitor (a key regulator of integrin signaling) to downregulate CD18 expression35, thereby suppressing leukocyte adhesion, migration, and peripheral inflammation in ischemic stroke model mice. The encapsulation efficiency of Pic@stiff reached at 68.52 ± 2.32 % (Fig. S10a). We employed Pic@stiff to suppress immune cell migration, like neutrophils, into the brain. As outlined in Fig. 4a, the primary neutrophils isolated from mice could penetrate the in vitro BBB model, followed by N-Formyl-Met-Leu-Phe (fMLP) stimulation to induce inflammation. The Pic@stiff treatment significantly reduced CD18 expression on neutrophils, thereby markedly decreasing their transmigration into the lower chamber under inflammatory conditions (Fig. 4b, c). Meanwhile, NBP36,37, a neuroprotectant targeting oxidative stress and apoptosis, was encapsulated in the soft NPs (NBP@soft), achieving an encapsulation efficiency of 77.42 ± 4.89% (Fig. S10b). 3. Why the Pic was loaded in PLGA NP instead of lipid layer outside?
Thank you very much for your question regarding the rationale of loading Piceatannol (Pic) into the PLGA core instead of the outer lipid layer, which indeed plays a crucial role in the therapeutic performance of our system.
There are two main considerations for this design:
1. Physicochemical compatibility and stability.
According to physicochemical data available from related databases (e.g. Drugbank), Pic exhibits a log P value of approximately 2.1 - 3.1, suggesting that it is a moderately hydrophobic small molecule. Previous studies have shown that small-molecule drugs with log P values in the range of 2 - 4 are preferentially encapsulated within PLGA NPs, where the hydrophobic polymer matrix can form stable intermolecular interaction with the drug molecules. This improved encapsulation efficiency and stability, while also reducing premature release of surface adsorption effects.
2. Fabrication and encapsulation efficiency:
In our fabrication process, the PLGA NPs were prepared via nanoprecipitation (NPR), due to its simplicity and efficiency. Then we utilized microfluidics to prepare Lipid coated PLGA NPs (Lipo-PLGA). The nanoprecipitation step allows straightforward co-dissolution and co-precipitation of hydrophobic drugs like Pic with PLGA in the organic phase, yielding high drug-loading efficiency and uniform entrapment within the polymeric matrix.
If Pic was instead added during the microfluidics stage, it could interfere with the self-assembly of the lipid monolayer on the PLGA surface, leading to impaired core-shell formation and reduced loading efficiency.
Drug release profiles of PLGA included four release mechanisms, containing diffusion through polymerc shells (governing the early stage of release) and degradation (as the particles degrade in the late stage). This phenomenon is well-documented in PLGA related literature (Sci. Rep., 2025,1:4218; Int. J. Pharm., 2006,314:198–206). This early fast-release window is compatible with the acute inflammation peak (6–24 h) following ischemic stroke.
Our dual-stiffness system utilized a core-shell structure for the stiff NPs (Lipo-PLGA NPs), where we desired to leverage the release profiles of PLGA NPs. This feature is highly advantageous for treating acute ischemic stroke, as the inflammation cascade peaks rapidly (typically 6–24 hours post-stroke). Specifically, because Pic is encapsulated within the PLGA core during preparation, Pic@stiff displayed both an initial burst release and a subsequent sustained-release phase (Fig. S11a). This profile is crucial for maintaining stable peripheral immune suppression during the early inflammatory surge. If Pic were instead added during the microfluidic lipi-coating process, it would likely remain primarily associated with the lipid layer and undergo only a rapid release, without the sustained phase. Such a pattern would be insufficient to provide prolonged modulation of the peripheral immune system during the acute ischemic stroke.

In summary, our approach of encapsulating Pic within the PLGA core is a deliberate strategy to maximize drug loading and stability while ensuring a controlled release profile, which is essential for its therapeutic application.

5. This article uses Lipo-PLGA as stiff NP (Young's modulus of 14.08 ± 3.23 GPa) and Liposome as soft NP (Young's modulus of 439.19 ± 82.06 kPa). What other NPs can be considered as stiff NP or soft NP? What is the range of their Young's modulus?
Thank you for this important question regarding the classification of NPs by their mechanical properties. In general, NPs can be categorized by their Young’s modulus: soft NPs such as liposomes, polymeric micelles, and hydrogel-based nanogels typically exhibit modulus ranging from several tens of kPa to several MPa, whereas stiff NPs such as PLGA NPs, silica NPs, and metallic or ceramic nanocarriers usually fall within hundreds of MPa to several GPa range.
It is crucial to note, as your question implies, that the precise boundary between “soft” and “stiff” is not universally defined. The reported values vary substantially across the literature due to differences in material composition, fabrication methods, and measurement approaches (e.g., Atomic Force Microscopy). For instance: Nature Communications (2018) demonstrated that NPs with Young’s moduli between 5 and 110 MPa displayed distinct cellular uptake and tumor penetration behaviors. Advanced Science (2020) reported stiffness-dependent interactions within the range of 60 MPa–1.41 GPa, while work from our group in Science Advances (2020) visualized the dynamic binding and internalization of NPs spanning 560 kPa–1.18 GPa.
In this study, we selected liposomes (439.19 ± 82.06 kPa) and Lipo-PLGA (14.08 ± 3.23 GPa) to represent the two mechanical extremes. This wide contrast (spanning nearly five orders of magnitude) provides a robust system to investigate the mechanobiological effects of NPs stiffness on drug delivery performance.
6. Why dose the substantial deformation of soft NPs result in delayed internalization? Is there any corresponding research that can prove this result?
Thank you very much for your questions. In our previous study, we have directly observed the cellular internalization process of NPs with different stiffness using single-particle tracking and TEM (Science Advances, 2020,6:eaaz4316). It was found that stiff NPs maintained their spherical morphology throughout both the membrane binding and internalization processes, whereas the soft one displayed substantial deformation during these stages, representative TEM images shown below (Sci. Adv., 2020, Fig.3B, Fig. S6).
Based on these established findings, we hypothesized that substantial deformation of soft NPs result in delayed internalization. To further support this hypothesis, we performed simulation using a coarse-grained molecular dynamics (CGMD) approach and tried to mimic more closely in this research. In this model, two types of NPs were designed to mimic the experimental setup: the soft NPs were modeled as lipid bilayer vesicles with no core, while the stiff NPs featured a PLGA core represented as a solid sphere, encapsulated by a lipid monolayer, which are almost the same as NPs used in this research (Fig. 2i). The free energy profile was obtained by integrating the spring force over the NP trajectory. Prior to membrane contact, the spring is compressed due to the NP’s free fall, performing positive work. From initial adhesion (~13 nm) to full immersion (~-12 nm), the spring extends against membrane deformation, resulting in a progressive increase in free energy cost. Notably, although soft NP exhibited a modest free energy benefit during early adhesion, full uptake required significantly greater penetration depth (43.6 nm), leading to a total energy cost of 538.8 𝑘 𝑇, being nearly double that of rigid NP (274.6 𝑘 𝑇). Simulations trajectories revealed that soft NP promote wrapping through persistent membrane neck elongation, suggesting that its compliance necessitates higher local membrane curvature and greater deformation energy (Fig. 2j,k). The setup enabled the assessment of the kinetic effects of the stiffnesses of the NPs on the uptake process. The simulation results confirmed that soft NPs indeed undergo noticeable deformation upon contact with immune cells, which could result in delayed uptake.
